classification: proposed semantic grouping; clauses retained verbatim, not independently course verified
precedence_note: Proposed engineering safeguard; referral does not authorize disclosure of restricted data. No group overrides medical or authorization requirements.

clauses.wording: Profile before prescription: create a multidimensional athlete profile before generating training.
Profile before prescription.
Treat body mass as functional mass relative to role; track it with composition and performance rather than assuming bigger is better.
Bigger, stronger, or leaner is not automatically better; physical development must remain functional.
Store absolute and relative strength because both can matter in rugby.
Store power as a distinct quality; power reflects force expressed at velocity.
Separate acceleration from maximal sprint speed and preserve split/test context.
Separate aerobic fitness, RSA, and RHIE instead of one generic endurance score.
Rugby performance depends on multiple physical qualities, not one fitness quality.
Strength, power, speed, and endurance must be assessed separately even though they interact.
Physical requirements vary by position and playing level.
Training should target gaps between the player’s current profile and required profile.
Training decisions should consider both team requirements and individual requirements.
Readiness is contextual and longitudinal: sleep, fatigue, soreness, stress, mental fatigue, mood, fueling and hydration inform but do not diagnose.
Lifestyle factors influence readiness, recovery, and adaptation.
Lifestyle monitoring should guide conversation and coaching decisions, not diagnose or judge the athlete.
Treat social-media/cognitive-load information as optional context, never surveillance.
Use privacy-by-design, especially for minors and sensitive health information.
Individualize nutrition; use food-first practice, carb periodization where useful, and anti-doping/supplement-contamination safeguards. Do not hard-code a 45-minute anabolic window.
Nutrition, recovery, and conditioning should all be individualized where practical.
Distinguish global movement screens, local joint ROM, and dynamic control under speed/load/repetition.
Screening should progress from broad observation toward more specific testing.
ROM tests provide local joint-level information.
Dynamic tests show how the athlete controls movement under more demanding conditions.
Screening produces observations and hypotheses, not medical diagnosis.
Use 'possible contributor', 'suggests', 'may contribute' and 'consistent with'; do not assert unmeasured causal muscle diagnoses.
Treat 'overactive/underactive' labels as hypotheses only; video observes movement, not muscle activation.
A movement finding generates hypotheses; it does not prove a muscular cause.
Pain is a hard gate: stop the automated corrective pathway and refer appropriately.
Pain changes the pathway from coaching/correction to medical review.
Store protocol, side, result, units, pain, asymmetry, date, assessor, intervention and retest date.
Standardize camera position, height, distance, athlete orientation, landmarks, repetition/frame, surface and footwear.
Store vision-derived measures with confidence and image-quality flags.
Every assessment must be standardized enough to allow reliable longitudinal comparison.
Repeated consistent findings increase hypothesis confidence; conflicting findings reduce it.
Repeated findings across different assessments strengthen a working hypothesis.
Secondary isolation tests should be used to confirm or challenge suspected contributors.
Match intervention to the identified limitation; stretching alone does not solve strength/control deficits.
Corrective interventions should match the actual limitation: mobility, strength, stability/control, or technique.
The original test should be repeated after intervention to verify whether the athlete actually improved.
